children.note: How the law governs selling goods, buying on hire purchase and acting for others (agency) in Kenya. A draft study aid for review, not legal advice.

children.note: The law of buying, selling and paying in business. It grows out of contract law from Year 1, with special rules for goods, credit and people who act for others.
Every sale, hire purchase deal or agency starts as a contract. Commercial law adds extra rules on top of the basic contract rules you learnt in Year 1.
From a duka selling sugar to a bank financing a matatu, trade depends on clear rules about who owns goods, who carries loss and who can sign for whom.
The Council of Legal Education lists this course as Commercial Law including sale of goods, hire purchase and agency. Those three are the heart of this map.

manas.q: Which three topics does the CLE core course on Commercial Law expressly include?

children.note: Kenya's commercial statutes were modelled on older English Acts, so English cases are often cited as persuasive. Kenyan Acts and courts have the final word in Kenya.
A sale of goods is a contract where the seller transfers ownership of goods to the buyer for money (the price). The Sale of Goods Act sets the default rules.
How a sale of goods contract comes into being and what counts as goods and price.
Ownership of goods passes for a money price. Swapping goods for goods (barter) or hiring them is not a sale.

manas.q: What two things make a contract a 'sale of goods'?

children.note: In a sale, ownership passes now. In an agreement to sell, it passes later or when a condition is met, for example when a farmer's maize is harvested.
Movable things you can touch: a phone, a cow, a bag of cement. Land and money are not goods.
Usually agreed by the parties. If no price is fixed, the buyer generally pays a reasonable price.
If specific goods have already perished when the contract is made, without the seller knowing, the contract is usually void. Perishing later may end an agreement to sell.
Promises the law reads into every sale even if no one said them out loud.
A condition is a major term: breach lets the buyer reject the goods. A warranty is a minor term: breach gives only damages.

manas.q: What is the difference between a condition and a warranty in a sale of goods?

children.note: The seller promises they have the right to sell. Selling a stolen motorbike breaks this term.

manas.q: What does the implied term as to title promise?

children.note: Goods sold by description must match it. 'Pishori rice' must be pishori. Reliance on the description matters.

manas.q: Under the implied term on description, what must goods do?

children.note: A business seller's goods must be of decent quality. Kenya's older-style Act speaks of merchantable quality; England now uses 'satisfactory quality'. Only business sellers are bound.

manas.q: Which implied term uses the phrase 'merchantable quality' in older-style Acts like Kenya's?

children.note: If the buyer tells a business seller what the goods are for and relies on their skill, the goods must be fit for that purpose.
When you buy from a sample, the bulk must match the sample and you must have a fair chance to compare them.
Sellers sometimes try to exclude these terms in small print. Courts read such clauses strictly, and consumer law limits them, especially against consumers.
Property means ownership. Risk means who bears the loss if goods are damaged. The timing of both matters a lot.
The parties decide when ownership passes. If they say nothing, the Act gives default rules.

manas.q: What is the main rule on when property in goods passes?

children.note: Specific goods are identified at the contract, like 'this red car'. Unascertained goods, like '50 bags of sugar from the store', cannot pass until they are identified.

manas.q: Why can property in unascertained goods not pass at once?

children.note: By default, whoever owns the goods carries the risk of loss, even if the other party holds them. Parties can agree otherwise.

manas.q: By default, who bears the risk of loss of goods?

children.note: A seller can agree to keep ownership until full payment. This is a retention of title (Romalpa) clause, useful when a buyer goes insolvent.
General rule: a seller who does not own goods cannot pass ownership, even to an honest buyer. The real owner keeps title.
If a thief sells your phone at a market, the buyer does not become owner. You can claim it back.

manas.q: What does the nemo dat rule say?

children.note: If the owner's words or conduct led the buyer to believe the seller could sell, the owner may be stopped (estopped) from denying it.
A rogue who gets goods by fraud has voidable title. If they sell to an honest buyer before the owner cancels the deal, the buyer gets good title.

manas.q: When can a buyer from a fraudster with voidable title keep the goods?

children.note: A dealer trusted with the owner's goods may pass good title to an honest buyer in the ordinary course of business.

children.topic: Exception: seller or buyer in possession
children.note: A seller who keeps goods after selling, or a buyer who gets them before owning them, may sometimes pass title to an honest third person.
England abolished the old open-market exception in 1995. Students should check the Kenyan Act's text before relying on it in Kenya.
What each side must do, and what happens when one fails.
The seller must deliver the goods; the buyer must accept them and pay. Unless agreed otherwise, the two happen together.
A buyer who says they accept, acts like the owner, or keeps goods too long without complaint loses the right to reject, but can still claim damages.

manas.q: How can a buyer lose the right to reject goods?

children.note: Sue for the price, claim damages if the buyer refuses to accept, and as an unpaid seller hold onto goods (lien), stop them in transit or resell in some cases.

manas.q: Name two remedies of an unpaid seller.

children.note: Reject the goods for breach of condition, claim damages for non-delivery or poor goods, and rarely ask the court to order delivery (specific performance).
Buying on instalments where you hire the goods first and become owner only when you finish paying. Common for cars, matatus and farm machines in Kenya.
You pay a deposit, use the goods and pay instalments. Ownership passes at the end, often by a small option-to-buy payment.

manas.q: When does a hirer under hire purchase become the owner?

children.note: Often a dealer sells the car to a finance company, which then lets it on hire purchase to you. Your contract is with the finance company.

children.topic: Not the same as a sale
children.note: Under hire purchase you are a hirer, not an owner, until the end. So you generally cannot sell the goods and pass good title meanwhile.

manas.q: Why can a hirer usually not pass good title before paying in full?

children.note: Pay off early, usually with a rebate; return the goods subject to limits; and sue if the owner wrongly repossesses.
If the hirer defaults, the owner may keep instalments paid, claim money due and repossess. The law can require a court order first.
Kenya has a Hire Purchase Act that sets formal rules for these agreements and protects hirers, for example on repossession. Read the Act itself for the exact thresholds.
One person (the agent) acts for another (the principal) to make deals with third parties. Think of a shop manager ordering stock for the owner.
Principal: the boss. Agent: the one acting. Third party: the outsider who deals with the agent. Three relationships arise.
By agreement, by later approval (ratification), by necessity in emergencies, or by the principal's conduct (estoppel).
The usual way: the principal appoints the agent, in writing or by word of mouth.
An agent acts without authority, and the principal later approves the act. The approval works backwards as if authority existed.

manas.q: What is ratification in agency?

children.note: In an emergency, a person holding another's goods may act to save them when they cannot reach the owner.
Authority decides whether the principal is bound.
Authority truly given, either in words (express) or understood from the job (implied).

manas.q: What two forms can actual authority take?

children.note: The principal makes it look as if the agent has authority, the third party relies on it, and the principal is bound.

manas.q: What three things must be shown for apparent (ostensible) authority?

children.note: A principal may be bound by acts usually within an agent's type of job, even if privately forbidden. The leading case is much criticised.
Obey instructions, use care and skill, act personally, avoid conflicts of interest, take no secret profit and account for money.

manas.q: Name three duties an agent owes the principal.

children.note: Pay the agreed commission and reimburse proper expenses.

children.topic: Who is liable to the third party
children.note: Usually the principal, if the agent acted within authority. An agent who claims authority they lack can be personally liable.
By agreement, finishing the task, or by law, such as death, insanity or bankruptcy of a party.
Where Kenyan commercial law comes from: the Constitution, Acts of Parliament and the courts.

Consumers have rights to goods and services of reasonable quality, to information, to protection of health, safety and money, and to compensation for loss or injury. Parliament must make consumer laws.

manas.q: Which Article of the Constitution of Kenya 2010 protects consumer rights?

children.note: Protects the right to own property and bars arbitrary taking. It is a reminder that ownership of goods is a protected right.
Kenya's main statute on sale of goods. It follows the older English model, so English cases on similar words are often persuasive.
Governs hire purchase agreements in Kenya, including their form and the hirer's protections.
Protects consumers against unfair and misleading business practices. It builds on Article 46 and sits alongside the Sale of Goods Act.
Cheques and bills of exchange can pass from hand to hand. An honest holder who pays value can take free of earlier defects, an exception to nemo dat.
Add the leading Kenyan decisions from Kenya Law (kenyalaw.org).
Classic common-law cases taught in Kenyan commercial law courses. They are persuasive, not binding, in Kenya.
A man got dermatitis from new woollen underwear. The Privy Council held the shop liable on fitness for purpose because he relied on its skill, and the maker liable in negligence.

manas.q: What did Grant v Australian Knitting Mills decide about the retailer?

children.note: A rogue posed as a known firm by letter. The contract was void for mistaken identity, so the honest later buyer got no title and returned the goods.

manas.q: Why did the innocent buyer lose in Cundy v Lindsay?

children.note: A car owner paid by a bad cheque told the police and AA at once. This clear act cancelled the voidable deal before the car reached a later buyer.

manas.q: How did Mr Caldwell rescind the contract with a vanished fraudster?

children.note: A supplier kept ownership of foil until paid. When the buyer became insolvent, the supplier recovered its unused foil and sale proceeds ahead of other creditors.

manas.q: What did the Romalpa case decide about retention of title clauses?

children.note: A pub owner was liable for cigars ordered by his manager, though privately forbidden, because such orders were usual for a manager. Heavily criticised today.

manas.q: Why was the owner liable in Watteau v Fenwick?

children.note: Apparent authority works like estoppel: a representation, reliance on it, and a change of position by the third party.
A painting was wrongly described, but the expert buyer had not relied on the description, so the description term was not breached.
Use IRAC: Issue, Rule, Application, Conclusion. Take each party and each issue in turn.
Wanjiru lends her motorbike to Otieno to repair. Otieno sells it to Kamau at a Kiambu market. Kamau paid fair value and suspected nothing. Can Wanjiru recover it?
Did Kamau get good title from someone who did not own the motorbike?
Nemo dat: no one passes better title than they have, subject to exceptions such as estoppel and the mercantile agent rule.
Otieno owned nothing. Was he a dealer acting in the ordinary course of business? Did Wanjiru's conduct mislead Kamau? Probably not on these facts.
Wanjiru can likely recover the motorbike; Kamau's claim is against Otieno. Always say what more facts could change the answer.
Points that lose marks easily.
Holding goods is not owning them. Ask who owns, not who holds.
Quality and fitness terms bind only sellers acting in the course of business, not your neighbour selling an old sofa.
A void contract (Cundy) passes no title; a voidable one (fraud face to face) can pass title until cancelled. Say which applies.

children.topic: Treating hire purchase as a sale
children.note: A hirer is not yet owner. This changes nemo dat and repossession answers.
Cite the Kenyan Act and Article 46 before English cases. English cases persuade; they do not bind Kenyan courts.
